objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer:
The objection deserves a careful answer, because it raises a real question—textual transmission—and then answers it wrongly by inverting the evidence. Let's look at what the manuscripts actually show, not what the New World Translation asserts.

First, on P52 (c. AD 125) and P66/P75 (c. 200), we already possess John's Gospel with "the Word was God" (1:1), "only-begotten God" (1:18), and Thomas' "My Lord and my God" (20:28) — more than a century before Nicaea, and within a generation or two of the apostles themselves. There is no manuscript tradition, however early, that lacks these readings and shows them being progressively inserted. The "a god" rendering isn't a manuscript variant at all; it's a translation choice by one denomination's committee, not something found in any Greek text. If scribes were smoothing the text toward higher Christology, we'd expect to find the raw, lower material in the earliest witnesses and the exalted material appearing later — but that's precisely backward from what P52 and the papyri show us.

Second, you're right that John 14:28 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 remain in the text, sitting alongside "the Word was God" — and this is not evidence against corruption but evidence against a simple binitarian-to-Trinitarian evolutionary model altogether, because both kinds of texts are early and both were preserved by the same believing communities without felt contradiction. That's the real historical datum: the earliest Christians held together Jesus' full humanity, his obedience to and sending by the Father, and his identity as God, without needing to erase one side to protect the other. Orthodoxy doesn't ask you to ignore "the Father is greater than I" — it explains it: as Son incarnate, Jesus speaks from within the personal order and the limits of his assumed humanity, not as a lesser divine nature.

Third, the scholarly consensus you invoke against an "evolutionary model" actually supports the opposite of your conclusion. Hurtado and Bauckham showed that worship of Jesus — prayer, hymns, invocation of his name — erupted among Jewish monotheists within the earliest years, before any Gentile "corruption" could have occurred. The highest Christology is also the earliest Christology, and it is Jewish to its bones, not a later Greek overlay.

Finally, on Mark's apparent restraint: this is an argument from silence, not from variants, and Mark still records Jesus forgiving sins as only God can (2:5-10), stilling the sea, and receiving the confession that he is the Christ, the Son of God (1:1). Silence in one Gospel's emphasis is not evidence of a text under construction; it's evidence of an author's chosen focus. The manuscript record itself gives no foothold for the corruption theory — it gives us, remarkably early, the very texts on which the case for Christ's deity rests.
